newsitem.title: UK: UK's Major's toughest election battle in own party.
newsitem.headline: UK's Major's toughest election battle in own party.

text.p: With just two weeks left before Britain's election, Prime Minister John Major is failing to make headway in opinion polls and is finding his toughest battleground is in his own Conservative Party.
An opinion poll in Thursday's Times showed support for Major's Conservatives slipped two points to 32 percent in the last week, putting the opposition Labour Party 17 points ahead.
The dip in fortunes traced the Conservatives' mood, which lifted last week when it finally began to make dents in Labour's formidable electioneering.

But by Wednesday, Major was on the back foot, forced to issue a dramatic appeal to voters to listen to him before Conservative rebels who have rejected his "wait and see" policy on joining a single European currency.
In a hastily recorded television message, Major implored voters not to "tie his hands" in negotiations for the currency by rejecting it now.
He was forced into the appeal, and into re-focusing his morning news conference, by the defiance of two junior ministers' who said in election statements they would oppose monetary union.
Labour claims another two Conservative junior ministers were also breaching the party line on European Union.
The rebellion brought to the fore an issued that has plagued Major throughout his 6-1/2 years as prime minister and touched on one of the trickiest election issues.
The MORI poll in The Times showed that if a referendum were held now, 58 percent of voters would oppose Britain joining a single currency compared with 22 percent who would favour it.
But Labour's line on monetary union, though barely distinguishable from Major's, appears to have done it little harm.
Even allowing for statistical error, if current opinion polls were translated into votes at the election, Blair's party would have a 100-seat majority in the 659-seat parliament.
Although there are clearly divisions within Labour, Blair has been spectacularly successful at preventing rebellions from within its senior ranks.
"I feel sorry for John Major," the Labour leader was able to say on Wednesday.

Major's failure to sack the rebellious junior ministers was proof, said Blair, of his inability to lead his party or the country. He had said the same two weeks ago when Conservative leaders were unable to force the resignation of a party candidate embroiled in influence-peddling allegations.

Despite having been so seriously wrongfooted, Major refuses to brook any possibility of defeat. In Wednesday's broadcast, he allowed no doubt that he would be the man to negotiate Britain's future in Europe.
"I will negotiate for Britain in these negotiations... I am therefore in a different position from anybody else in this country when I conduct those negotiations," he asserted.
By contrast, Blair has never allowed himself to be complacent about his chances of bringing the Conservatives' 18 years of rule to an end.
Twice this week, he has appeared to have broken his self-imposed rule and admitted the possibility that he could win the May 1 election and he has immediately qualified his words.

Meanwhile, Blair's aides, while welcoming Major's discomfiture, are unhappy that the wrangling in the ruling party has, like the row over sleaze that dominated the campaign earlier, detracted from discussion of policy.
The Labour leader made one of a series of major policy speeches on Wednesday, outlining "Seven Pillars of a Decent Society." It went largely unreported.
